stops.name: 6 Harvey Road, Cambridge: the house of the two Keyneses
stops.date_confidence: attested; MacTutor and the King's College biography agree on the date and the address. The coordinate is a street-level estimate for Harvey Road, Petersfield (OSM/Nominatim, CB1 2ET), not a rooftop geocode.
stops.campa: At six Harvey Road, in a house belonging to the university rather than to trade, Florence Ada Keynes gives birth to a first son on the fifth of June. His father John Neville Keynes lectures in logic and political economy and will outlive him. The household is Nonconformist, careful, and organised around examinations; his mother will in time become mayor of Cambridge. The boy is registered John Maynard Keynes. Harvey Road runs half a mile from the gate of King's College.

stops.name: St Faith's School, Trumpington Road: the boy ahead of the class
stops.date_confidence: attested for the schooling (MacTutor gives kindergarten then St Faith's, c.1889-1897); the month and day are a placeholder. The pin is St Faith's on the Trumpington Road; the earlier kindergarten was a separate establishment and is not pinned here.
stops.campa: He is sent first to a kindergarten and then to St Faith's on the Trumpington Road, where the masters report the same thing in different words: the boy is far ahead of the others and knows it. He is delicate, often ill, and reads faster than he is taught. His father keeps a written record of his progress, term by term. Nothing in the record suggests a child straining. The strain is all in the household around him, arranging the next examination before the last one has been marked.
suggested_refs: St Faith's School, 6 Trumpington Road, Cambridge
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'John Maynard Keynes'

stops.name: Eton College, Windsor: the King's Scholar
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1897 by MacTutor, which also gives 'ranked tenth of twenty accepted boys' and 'first equal in mathematics'; the September start is the school calendar, not a documented date. The Tomline Prize is dated 1901 by Wikipedia, cross-checked against MacTutor.
stops.campa: He wins a King's Scholarship to Eton in 1897 and enters tenth of the twenty boys accepted, placed first equal in mathematics. Eton takes a Cambridge don's son and hands back a collector and a debater, a snob of a particular English kind, at ease among the sons of the governing class and quicker than most of them. He carries off the Tomline Prize for mathematics in 1901. Daniel Macmillan, of the publishing family, is the friend he attaches himself to here, the first of several.
stops.quote_source: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'John Maynard Keynes', on his Eton entrance placing

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: the scholar and the twelfth Wrangler
stops.date_confidence: attested; MacTutor gives October 1902, the scholarship in mathematics and classics, E. W. Hobson as tutor, and twelfth Wrangler in 1905. The Marshall detail below is standard biography rather than a claim verified in this research pass.
stops.campa: In October he comes up to King's on a scholarship in mathematics and classics, tutored by E. W. Hobson, and thereafter leaves the college only to work in London. He reads mathematics for the Tripos and is placed twelfth Wrangler in 1905, a good result and not a great one. Alfred Marshall presses him to become an economist. He attends lectures in the subject for a matter of weeks, the whole of his formal training in the discipline he will remake, and turns instead to philosophy, to Moore's Principia Ethica, and to the societies.

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: the Apostles elect him
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1903 by King's College's own account of the Cambridge Conversazione Society; the day is a placeholder. The Society met in members' rooms, so the pin is the college, not a room.
stops.campa: In February he is elected to the Cambridge Conversazione Society, twelve undergraduates who call themselves the Apostles and meet on Saturday nights to read papers to one another. Lytton Strachey and Leonard Woolf are already members. What Keynes takes from it is G. E. Moore's ethics, states of mind as the only good, friendship and beauty ranked above duty, and he keeps it privately for the rest of his life. It is the one secret society of his biography that college records actually document. He is nineteen.
suggested_refs: King's College Cambridge, 'Cambridge secret revealed: the Apostles'

segments.name: The India Office and the Return to King's

stops.name: India Office, Whitehall: second in the examination
stops.date_confidence: attested; MacTutor gives the August 1906 examination, the second place, the India Office posting instead of the Treasury, economics as his lowest paper, and the October 1906 start. The remark about knowing more than his examiners is repeated in the standard biographies and is not independently verified here.
stops.campa: He sits the Civil Service examination in August 1906 and comes second of all candidates, which is not first, and so he is sent to the India Office rather than to the Treasury he wanted. His lowest mark of all is in economics. He tells friends he knew more about the subject than his examiners did. From October he works in Whitehall on military and financial administration for a subcontinent he will never visit. The machinery of the gold-exchange standard he learns from files, two thousand miles from the thing itself.
suggested_refs: India Office records, Whitehall, 1906-1908
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'John Maynard Keynes'

stops.name: India Office, Whitehall: the resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested; MacTutor gives 5 June 1908 for the resignation, boredom with routine and the probability dissertation as the reasons. That the date is also his twenty-fifth birthday follows from the 1883-06-05 birth date and is noted here as arithmetic, not as a documented remark of his.
stops.campa: Two years of minutes and dispatch boxes are enough. On the fifth of June 1908, his twenty-fifth birthday, he resigns, bored by the routine and impatient to finish the dissertation on probability that Cambridge has not yet paid him to write. Marshall has offered a lectureship funded out of his own pocket. Keynes leaves the India Office without a salary, carrying an unfinished manuscript, and takes the train north. He does not hold a government post again for seven years.
suggested_refs: Keynes's letter of resignation from the India Office, June 1908
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'John Maynard Keynes'

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: the fellowship on probability
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1909 by MacTutor and the King's biography; the day is a placeholder. The Political Economy Club is dated 'from 1909' on weaker authority and is carried here as reconstruction.
stops.campa: He revises the dissertation twice and is elected a Fellow of King's in March 1909, on a theory that probability is a logical relation between a body of evidence and a conclusion, degrees of rational belief rather than frequencies counted in the world. The same year he founds the Political Economy Club, where undergraduates read papers on Monday evenings and are taken apart in front of each other. He is a Fellow of the college, a lecturer paid by Marshall, and an editor within two years. The manuscript itself waits twelve more.
suggested_refs: Keynes's King's College fellowship dissertation on probability, 1908-09
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'John Maynard Keynes'

stops.name: Cambridge: the Economic Journal
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1911, held until 1945 (MacTutor; Wikipedia); month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: At twenty-eight he takes the editorship of the Economic Journal for the Royal Economic Society and holds it for thirty-four years, until 1945. Nearly everything written in English on the subject crosses his desk on its way into print, refereed in his own hand and frequently rewritten. He acquires by this route an exact map of what the profession believes and where it is weak, which is not the knowledge a man gets from a chair. At this date he is still an orthodox quantity theorist and edits as one.
suggested_refs: The Economic Journal under Keynes's editorship, 1911-1945

stops.name: Westminster: the Royal Commission on Indian Finance and Currency
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book (1913) and for membership of the Commission (1913-14, Wikipedia, which states he was appointed to it and calls it 'the same topic as his book'). CONTRADICTION FLAGGED: one source in the research pool called him the Commission's secretary; that post was Basil Blackett's, and the correction to 'member, its youngest' is followed here. That he drafted the bulk of the report is standard biography, not verified in this pass.
stops.campa: His first book, Indian Currency and Finance, appears in 1913 on the gold-exchange standard he had administered from a desk in Whitehall, and it makes his name in the Treasury he had failed to enter. He is appointed to the Royal Commission on Indian Finance and Currency as its youngest member and drafts the bulk of its report, including an annexe proposing a state central bank for India that the Commission declines to adopt. Basil Blackett serves as its secretary. The report is finished in 1914 and overtaken by August.

segments.name: The Treasury, Bloomsbury, and the Peace

stops.name: HM Treasury, Great George Street: the war finance
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1915 (MacTutor; Wikipedia) for entry, and to 1917 for the CB (Wikipedia); the day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: In January 1915 he enters the Treasury in Great George Street on external war finance and stays four years. He manages the allied credits, the exchange controls and the purchase of foreign currency for a country buying a war on credit from America. He is the friend and defender of conscientious objectors in Bloomsbury and a servant of the war machine on weekdays, and he does not pretend that the two positions are one. In 1917 he is made a Companion of the Order of the Bath for the work.

stops.name: 46 Gordon Square, Bloomsbury: the London house
stops.date_confidence: attested; English Heritage's blue plaque at 46 Gordon Square is inscribed 'lived here 1916-1946', which fixes both address and start year. CONTRADICTION FLAGGED: the research pool initially carried 41 Gordon Square, which is not his; the plaque register and the OSM memorial node at 51.5244, -0.1302 are followed instead. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He takes the house at 46 Gordon Square, in the Bloomsbury square where Vanessa Bell, Duncan Grant and Lytton Strachey keep rooms, and holds it for thirty years, until his death. Here the two halves of the life are put in one room: Treasury officials at dinner with painters who will not fight. He buys pictures, argues about Moore's ethics, and goes back to Whitehall in the morning. Virginia Woolf, who is fond of him and merciless about him, records the arrivals in her diary.

stops.name: Charleston Farmhouse, near Firle: the Sussex weekends
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That Keynes was a frequent guest at Charleston from 1916 is well attested across Bloomsbury scholarship but was not confirmed from a primary source in this pass; the month and day are placeholders. The coordinate is OSM's for Charleston, Firle, BN8 6LL.
stops.campa: Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant take a farmhouse under the Downs near Firle and paint every surface in it. Keynes comes down from London for weekends and long summers, works in a room with a decorated fireplace, and keeps his own furniture there. Grant, once his lover, is the fixed point of the household. He will not leave this corner of Sussex again. Tilton, the farmhouse he eventually takes for himself, stands a walk across two fields from this door.
suggested_refs: Charleston Farmhouse, Firle, East Sussex, the Bell and Grant household

stops.name: Hotel Majestic, avenue Kleber, Paris: the Peace Conference
stops.date_confidence: attested that Keynes served as Treasury representative and deputy for the Chancellor on the Supreme Economic Council at Paris in 1919 (Wikipedia; King's College). RECONSTRUCTION on the pin: the Hotel Majestic housed the British delegation, but that Keynes's own office was there rather than at a Treasury annexe was not confirmed in this pass. The coordinate is OSM's for 19 avenue Kleber. Month and day are placeholders for the conference's opening.
stops.campa: He crosses to Paris as principal Treasury representative and deputy for the Chancellor on the Supreme Economic Council, and spends six months watching four men decide the shape of Europe. The British delegation works out of the Hotel Majestic on the avenue Kleber. He argues against the reparations figure in memorandum after memorandum, proposes a scheme of European reconstruction credits that no government will fund, and is beaten by the arithmetic of a French election and a British one. He watches Clemenceau in particular, and writes it down.
stops.quote: Clemenceau silent and aloof on the outskirts—for nothing which touched the security of France was forward—throned, in his gray gloves, on the brocade chair, dry in soul and empty of hope, very old and tired
stops.quote_source: J. M. Keynes, The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919), ch. III, 'The Conference'; Project Gutenberg 15776 (truncated from a longer sentence beginning 'and Clemenceau silent and aloof')
suggested_refs: The Hotel Majestic, 19 avenue Kleber, Paris, headquarters of the British delegation in 1919
sources: Wikipedia, 'John Maynard Keynes'

stops.name: HM Treasury, Great George Street: the resignation of 1919
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1919 (MacTutor; Wikipedia) as a resignation in protest at the scale of reparations demanded from Germany; the day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: In June he writes to the Chancellor that he can be of no further use here and goes home. The reparations figure has passed beyond anything Germany can pay and the Treasury will not fight it further. He is thirty-six and has resigned the second great office of his life on a point of judgment, having resigned the first out of boredom. He goes down to Sussex in a condition his friends call collapse. He begins writing within weeks, and the book is finished before the autumn is out.
suggested_refs: Keynes's June 1919 resignation from the Treasury delegation at Paris
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'John Maynard Keynes'

stops.name: 46 Gordon Square, Bloomsbury: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1919 for publication (MacTutor; Wikipedia); the day is a placeholder. The pin is his London house, not a documented place of composition; standard biography places much of the writing in Sussex.
stops.campa: The Economic Consequences of the Peace appears in December, a short book of economics with a few pages of portraiture in it, and sells in tens of thousands across a dozen languages. He tells Europe that the reparations are unpayable, that the treaty makes no provision whatever for the economic life of the continent it has redrawn, and that hunger and inflation will follow. The portraits of Wilson, Clemenceau and Lloyd George are what people quote. He is famous at thirty-six.
stops.quote: He had one illusion—France; and one disillusion—mankind, including Frenchmen, and his colleagues not least.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Keynes, The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919), ch. III, 'The Conference', on Clemenceau; Project Gutenberg 15776

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: A Treatise on Probability
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1921 (MacTutor; Wikipedia); month and day are placeholders. The Ramsey criticism is a dossier claim for which no corroborating atlas file exists and which was not independently verified in this pass; it is carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Twelve years after the fellowship dissertation, the book on probability finally appears. It argues that probability is a logical relation of partial entailment between evidence and conclusion, that some probabilities cannot be given a number at all, and that some cannot be compared with one another. Frank Ramsey, an undergraduate of the same college, takes the argument apart within a few years and Keynes concedes much of it. The unmeasurable stays with him, and turns up fifteen years later as the ground of the General Theory.
suggested_refs: J. M. Keynes, A Treatise on Probability (1921); F. P. Ramsey, 'Truth and Probability' (1926)

stops.name: 46 Gordon Square, Bloomsbury: A Tract on Monetary Reform
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1923 (MacTutor; Wikipedia); month and day are placeholders. The pin is his London house, not a documented place of composition. The famous sentence is quoted here from Wikiquote's sourced citation (ch. 3, p. 80): no full text of the Tract could be reached online in this pass, and the indirection is flagged rather than hidden.
stops.campa: He writes A Tract on Monetary Reform against the plan to put sterling back on gold at its prewar parity, arguing that stable domestic prices matter more than a fixed external one, and that the gold standard is already a relic in everything but name. The book contains the sentence that will be quoted against him for a century by people who have not read the paragraph it sits in, where the point is the opposite of recklessness: that economists who promise equilibrium in the long run have set themselves too easy a task.
stops.quote: But this long run is a misleading guide to current affairs. In the long run we are all dead.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Keynes, A Tract on Monetary Reform (1923), ch. 3, p. 80, cited via Wikiquote; primary text not reachable in this pass

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: First Bursar
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1924 for the First Bursarship, with the Second Bursarship from 1919 (King's College biography); month and day are placeholders. The National Mutual chairmanship (1921-1938) is carried as reconstruction from Wikipedia. The trading-from-bed detail is standard biography, not verified here.
stops.campa: Second Bursar of King's since 1919, he becomes First Bursar in 1924 and runs the college endowment until his death. He moves it out of land and fixed-interest stock and into ordinary shares, currencies and commodities, which no other Oxford or Cambridge bursar does, and trades in the mornings from bed by telephone. He is chairman of the National Mutual Life Assurance Society at the same time. He is nearly ruined in 1929 and again in 1937. The fund he leaves the college is several times the one he took over.

stops.name: 46 Gordon Square, Bloomsbury: The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1925 for the pamphlet (Wikipedia; MacTutor); the July date is the conventional one for publication and is not confirmed in the verified pool. The pin is his London house. The ten per cent overvaluation figure is his own estimate as reported in standard accounts, not verified here.
stops.campa: Churchill, as Chancellor, returns sterling to gold at the old parity in the April budget, and Keynes answers with a pamphlet that names him in the title. The parity overvalues the pound by roughly a tenth; the adjustment must therefore come out of wages, and it comes out of the coal industry first. He writes that the Chancellor has been misled by his experts and that the policy amounts to a deliberate intensification of unemployment. The coal lockout begins in the spring of 1926 and the General Strike follows it in May.
suggested_refs: J. M. Keynes, The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill (1925)

stops.name: St Pancras Register Office, London: marriage to Lydia Lopokova
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1925 (King's College biography: 'married Lydia Lopokova in 1925'). CONTRADICTION FLAGGED and unresolved: standard biographies give 4 August 1925, while some genealogical summaries give 7 August; neither could be confirmed against a primary record in this pass. The St Pancras register-office venue is plausible tradition, not confirmed, and the pin should be read accordingly.
stops.campa: He marries Lydia Lopokova, who danced for Sergei Diaghilev and left the Ballets Russes to live in Gordon Square with an economist ten years her senior. Bloomsbury is appalled, or amused, or both, and says so in letters he is not shown. The friends who predict a season are wrong by twenty-one years, and she is the one sitting with him at Tilton on the last morning. She calls him Maynarochka and writes him an English of her own construction, and he keeps every letter she sends.

stops.name: Moscow: A Short View of Russia
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 1925 Russian journey with Lydia and the resulting pamphlet are given by Wikipedia, but the month, day and itinerary were not confirmed in this pass. The pin is the Moscow city coordinate, not a specific address.
stops.campa: He travels to Russia with Lydia in the autumn, to her family and then to Moscow, and looks at planning at close range for the first time. A Short View of Russia follows. He judges communism an illogical creed, cruel in its methods and dishonest in its economics, and grants it the one thing he thinks capitalism lacks, an appeal to something other than the pursuit of money. Both halves of the judgment are in the pamphlet. He withdraws neither of them, then or afterwards.
suggested_refs: J. M. Keynes, A Short View of Russia (1925), collected in Essays in Persuasion

stops.name: 46 Gordon Square, Bloomsbury: The End of Laissez-Faire
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1926 for publication (Wikipedia). CORRECTION CARRIED: the research pool placed publication at Cambridge; the essay began as the 1924 Sidney Ball Lecture at Oxford and was published by the Hogarth Press in London, so the pin is his London house. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The lecture he gave at Oxford in 1924 is published by the Hogarth Press as The End of Laissez-Faire. He writes that the world is not so governed from above that private and social interest always coincide, and that it is not a correct deduction from the principles of economics that enlightened self-interest always operates in the public good. He rejects state socialism in the same pages as a misreading of what is actually wrong. What he proposes instead is a layer of semi-autonomous bodies inside the state, answerable but not directed.

stops.name: Westminster: Can Lloyd George Do It? and the Macmillan Committee
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1929 for both the pamphlet with Hubert Henderson and the Macmillan Committee on Finance and Industry (Wikipedia); the May date is the general election month and the day is a placeholder. The Westminster pin stands for the parliamentary and committee milieu rather than a single room.
stops.campa: With Hubert Henderson he writes Can Lloyd George Do It?, a pamphlet for the general election defending loan-financed public works against the Treasury view that such spending merely displaces private investment pound for pound. In the same year he is appointed to the Macmillan Committee on Finance and Industry and spends days in the witness chair explaining to bankers how a country can be shackled by its exchange rate and idle at the same time. Lloyd George loses the election. The unemployment figure passes a million and goes on rising.

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: A Treatise on Money
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1930 for the two-volume Treatise (MacTutor; Wikipedia) and to 1930 for 'Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren'; month and day are placeholders. The pin is Cambridge, where he worked; publication was in London. The Grandchildren quotation is taken from Wikiquote's citation, the essay's own full text having been unreachable in this pass.
stops.campa: After six years he publishes A Treatise on Money in two volumes: the fundamental equations, the wedge driven between saving and investment, the argument that prices move when the two fall out of step. It is the largest thing he has written and he is dissatisfied with it before the reviews arrive. The same year he writes a short essay guessing what his generation's grandchildren will do with an economic problem solved, and what they will make of money once they no longer need it.
stops.quote: The love of money as a possession—as distinguished from the love of money as a means to the enjoyments and realities of life—will be recognised for what it is, a somewhat disgusting morbidity, one of those semi-criminal, semi-pathological propensities which one hands over with a shudder to the specialists in mental disease.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Keynes, 'Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren' (1930), collected in Essays in Persuasion; cited via Wikiquote

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: a frightful muddle
stops.date_confidence: attested; Hayek's two-part Economica review ran August 1931 and February 1932, Sraffa's counterattack in the Economic Journal in 1932, and Hayek never reviewed the General Theory and later called the silence a regret. The pin is Keynes's own college, where he edited the Economic Journal, not the LSE milieu where Economica was produced. The day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Friedrich Hayek, brought to London from Vienna, reviews the Treatise on Money in Economica across two issues and finds the whole structure unsound. Keynes reads Hayek's Prices and Production in return and calls it a frightful muddle. He then hands the counterattack to Piero Sraffa, who publishes it in the Economic Journal, the journal Keynes himself edits. Neither man moves the other an inch. When the General Theory appears five years later Hayek writes no review of it at all, and later calls that silence a regret.
stops.quote_source: Keynes on Hayek's Prices and Production, as recorded in friedrich_hayek.journey.json; original print citation not re-verified in this pass
suggested_refs: F. A. Hayek, 'Reflections on the Pure Theory of Money of Mr J. M. Keynes', Economica, August 1931 and February 1932; P. Sraffa, Economic Journal, 1932

stops.name: 46 Gordon Square, Bloomsbury: the pound leaves gold
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1931 that Britain left the gold standard (Wikipedia, cross-checked against standard economic history); the twenty-first is the conventional date and is not confirmed in the verified pool. GAP: Keynes's own whereabouts on the day are not established, and the pin is his London house rather than a documented location.
stops.campa: In September the government suspends the gold standard, six years after putting sterling back on it and eight after he told them in print not to. The pound falls by about a quarter, exports revive, and none of the catastrophes the defenders of the parity had foretold arrives. He has been right in public, at length, and the rightness comes six years late, after the wage cuts and the lockout and the strike. He is already at work on the book that will explain why the orthodox account of it was wrong in the first place.

stops.name: New Statesman and Nation, London: answering Wells on Stalin
stops.date_confidence: attested; H. G. Wells interviewed Stalin in the Kremlin on 23 July 1934 and the New Statesman printed it in October 1934 'with replies from Shaw and Keynes printed alongside it'. The pin is the canonical London coordinate carried on the h_g_wells file for this episode, inherited unchanged. The exact issue date given here is the conventional one.
stops.campa: H. G. Wells goes to the Kremlin in July and talks to Stalin for three hours, and the New Statesman and Nation prints the transcript in October with replies from Bernard Shaw and from Keynes set alongside it. Keynes had chaired the board of the Nation and Athenaeum, the paper that merged into this one, and had used it for years to argue public works against the Treasury view. His reply to Wells defends neither Stalin nor the City. He is fifty-one, and is consulted now about the survival of the system rather than about its accounting.

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: The General Theory
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1936 (MacTutor; Wikipedia); the fourth of February is the standard publication date and is not confirmed in the verified pool. The Schumpeter detail is carried from joseph_schumpeter.journey.json, which dates his permanent Harvard chair to 1932 and records him promoting Keynesians whose conclusions he rejected.
stops.campa: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money is published in February, arguing that an economy can come to rest with men out of work and stay there, that the level of output is set by effective demand and not by the willingness of workers to accept lower wages, and that a government can therefore move it. Cambridge undergraduates read it in the term it appears. At Harvard, Joseph Schumpeter rejects its conclusions outright and trains the students who carry them across America regardless.
stops.quote: Most, probably, of our decisions to do something positive, the full consequences of which will be drawn out over many days to come, can only be taken as a result of animal spirits — of a spontaneous urge to action rather than inaction, and not as the outcome of a weighted average of quantitative benefits multiplied by quantitative probabilities.

stops.date_confidence: attested; the Newton Project dates the Sotheby sale to 13-14 July 1936 and states that Keynes 'failed to realise the full significance of what was on offer until the sale had been largely completed', then 'immediately set about buying up Newton manuscripts from both individuals and dealers', Maggs Brothers of London chief among them. stops.campa: The papers descended in the Portsmouth family from Isaac Newton are dispersed at Sotheby's over two days in July. Keynes does not grasp the full significance of what is on offer until the sale has largely been completed. He spends the years afterwards buying the alchemical and theological manuscripts back from individuals and from dealers, Maggs Brothers of London chief among them, reassembling by private purchase a collection the auction had broken into lots. Why an economist is buying them is a question he does not answer for another ten years.
stops.quote: Why do I call him a magician? Because he looked on the whole universe and all that is in it as a riddle, as a secret which could be read by applying pure thought to certain evidence, certain mystic clues which God had laid about the world to allow a sort of philosopher's treasure hunt to the esoteric brotherhood.

From here the day is rationed: an hour of work, then lying flat, then another hour, with Lydia holding the watch and turning callers away at the door. The eight years of work still in front of him, which are the war finance, the Bank, the Lords, Bretton Woods and the American loan, are all done from inside that regime.

stops.campa: The London School of Economics evacuates to Cambridge in the autumn of 1939 and Hayek is lodged at Peterhouse, a few hundred yards down Trumpington Street from King's. The two men who had divided English economics between them spend the war as neighbours, dining, arguing, and, by a recollection repeated ever since though no duty roster confirms it, fire-watching together on a college roof. The question between them is being settled elsewhere, by the war itself, in favour of the man from King's. Neither has moved his position since 1931.

stops.date_confidence: attested to 1940 for the pamphlet (MacTutor; Wikipedia's list of works); the February date is conventional and the day is a placeholder. That the 1941 budget was built on national income accounting is standard economic history rather than a claim verified in this pass.
stops.campa: He is back inside the Treasury as an adviser with a room and no defined post, and he publishes How to Pay for the War. Wages are to be taxed at source and part of the tax credited back to the worker as deferred pay, released after the peace, so that the inflation of the last war is not repeated and the burden falls where it is put rather than where it happens to land. The unions object and then accept a modified version. The budget that follows is drawn up on national income accounting for the first time.

stops.name: US Treasury Building, Washington: Lend-Lease and Harry Dexter White
stops.date_confidence: attested that Keynes crossed repeatedly to Washington from 1941 to negotiate Lend-Lease, postwar employment schemes and a new monetary order with American officials including Harry Dexter White (IMF institutional history, elibrary.imf.org). stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic in wartime, by flying boat and by ship, more often than his heart can stand, to negotiate in the corridors of the American Treasury with Harry Dexter White. Britain is spending its reserves and selling its American assets to fight, and will be insolvent on the day it wins. Keynes is charming and impatient by turns, and audibly cleverer than the room, which does him no good at all. Lend-Lease comes on terms that include the dismantling of imperial preference.

From these benches he will defend, against Conservative and Labour anger alike, the terms of an American loan he himself thinks harsh. He is fifty-nine, and this is the first seat in Parliament he has ever held.

His own plan, an international clearing union with a unit of account he calls bancor, penalising persistent creditors as well as persistent debtors, is not adopted. White's plan is. He drives his commission through its agenda at a pace the Americans find alarming. The Fund and the Bank are founded on the twenty-second of July in a shape he did not design, and he signs for them.

stops.name: Washington, D.C.: the Anglo-American Financial Agreement
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1945 that Keynes negotiated the Anglo-American Financial Agreement in Washington after the abrupt end of Lend-Lease (Wikipedia, without a precise date in the verified pool). The sixth of December is the conventional signing date and is not confirmed here; the two per cent rate, the convertibility clause and the 1947 collapse are standard economic history rather than pool-verified claims.
stops.campa: Lend-Lease stops within days of the Japanese surrender and Britain has weeks of dollars in hand. Keynes goes to Washington expecting something like a grant in recognition of the war and is offered a loan at interest, with sterling to be made convertible within a year of the agreement coming into force. He negotiates for three months, in failing health, against men who regard the whole transaction as commercial. The agreement is signed in December. Convertibility is attempted in the summer of 1947 and collapses in a matter of weeks.

stops.name: Savannah, Georgia: the inaugural meeting of the governors
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the detail. Savannah and March 1946 for the inaugural meeting of the IMF and World Bank governors are well attested in the general Keynes literature, but imf.org returned 403 in this research pass and no primary institutional source could be loaded to confirm venue detail. stops.campa: The governors of the Fund and the Bank meet for the first time at Savannah in March, and the argument is over where the two institutions will live and who will run them. Keynes wants them in New York, at arm's length from any treasury; the Americans put them in Washington. He wants part-time directors of standing; he gets full-time officials. The American secretary across the table is not Morgenthau and does not pretend to be friendly. He leaves having lost every point of substance, visibly failing, and sails for England.

stops.name: King's College, Cambridge: Newton, the Man
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Newton Project records that the lecture, prepared for the Newton tercentenary, was delivered posthumously by his brother Geoffrey Keynes after Maynard's death, and that Keynes bequeathed his Newton manuscripts to King's College, Cambridge. The month and day are placeholders for the tercentenary observance; the pool also names the Royal Society Club as the delivery setting, and that detail is not resolved here.
stops.campa: He had accepted the invitation to speak at the Newton tercentenary and had written the lecture out. The observance is postponed by the war, and by the time it is held he is three months dead. His brother Geoffrey reads it in his place. It is an economist's demolition of the official Newton: not the first of the age of reason but the last of the magicians, a man who read the universe as a cipher God had scattered about the world for an esoteric brotherhood to solve. The manuscripts he bought back from the dealers pass by his bequest to King's.
stops.quote: Newton was not the first of the age of reason. He was the last of the magicians, the last of the Babylonians and Sumerians, the last great mind which looked out on the visible and intellectual world with the same eyes as those who began to build our intellectual inheritance rather less than 10,000 years ago.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Keynes, 'Newton, the Man' (written for the 1946 Newton tercentenary, delivered by Geoffrey Keynes), text as reproduced by MacTutor History of Mathematics
